new_statements.quote: It is not clear whether something comparable to stress is appropriately identified in Meꞌphaa. However, there is evidence that words and phrases are prosodically right-headed. Rensch (1978:631) refers to the “tonic ultima”. Suárez (1983:26) likewise gives reasons for considering that, at least at an earlier stage of the language, the final syllable was accented. [...] First, as we have alluded to already, various phonetic details require reference to a weak syllable of the root. In a disyllabic root, the final syllable is strong and the first is weak. [...] The addition of an affix does not affect the basic prosodic structure; the root in the word continues to have a weak syllable followed by a strong one.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (pdfinfo: 'The sounds of Me'phaa (Tlapanec): A new assessment', Marlett & Weathers, XLingPaper, 31 pp., Oct 2018; title page cites SIL-Mexico Electronic Working Papers #25, archive 76311). extracted text of pp. 22-25: Section 7 'Prominence' begins on p. 23 and the quoted sentences are there word for word; the two '[...]' elisions skip (a) the Poser 1990 sentence on foot structure without a stress system and (b) the sentence on lenition / historical b>w, k>h substitutions in weak syllables and minor-class monosyllables. The closing sentence 'The addition of an affix does not affect the basic prosodic structure; the root in the word continues to have a weak syllable followed by…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Me'phaa (all varieties, Azoyú included in the sample) is a tone language (High, Mid, Low with one- and two-tone melodies on roots; for Azoyú Wichmann gives 3 level + 4 contour tones, normally confined to the last two syllables of the word). The authors decline to posit stress as such but state that prosody is right-headed: the final syllable of the root is the strong syllable and preceding syllables are weak (site of lenition, k>h, b>w, d>[r], vowel shortening/loss); affixes do not shift this, so the strong syllable is root-final, which in practice is word-final since suffixes fuse with the root-final vowel and prefixes are weak. If one codes the prominence as stress it is fixed final (iambic), quantity-insensitive.
new_statements.exceptions: No word-level exceptions to final strength are given. Monosyllabic minor-class words (discourse markers, subordinators) pattern as weak syllables; in lexicalized phrases and compounds the leftward syllables reduce; some contour melodies sit on monosyllables. For Azoyú specifically the authors note only that some words keep [d] in weak syllables (incomplete d>r change, p. 9) and that Azoyú tone melodies differ from the highland varieties (p. 22).
new_statements.domain_note: Claim is made for the Me'phaa genus as a whole ('words and phrases are prosodically right-headed'); domain of the weak/strong asymmetry is the root within the word, unaffected by affixation; data are citation forms. Wichmann's Azoyú-specific work adds that phonological tone is restricted to the last two syllables of the word (Wichmann 2010, conventions, prepub p. 22), consistent with a right-edge prosodic head, but he never describes stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source (Marlett & Weathers 2018) is a genus-wide assessment of Me'phaa covering ISO tcf, tpc, tpl and tpx; its Azoyú [tpc] data come from the towns of Azoyú [tpc-Azoy] and Zapotitlán de la Fuente [tpc-ZFue] (speaker Constantino Zavaleta Navor), and the prominence claim is stated for Me'phaa as a whole rather than separately for Azoyú. The Azoyú-specific describer (Wichmann 1992-2010, fieldwork in Azoyú town) gives only tone facts (3 level + 4 contour tones, tone confined to the last two syllables) and never mentions stress. Cornelio Tiburcio 2022, the only instrumental stress study of Me'phaa, describes Ciénega del Sauce (mun. Ayutla de los Libres), which INALI and Marlett & Weathers treat as an Acatepec-type variety (approx. Glottolog acat1239), not Azoyú. The catalog already holds acat1239 from Marlett & Neri Remigio 2012 with the same family-level 'iambic, final syllable strong, no stress identified' note; the azoy1236 entry would rest on the same authors' 2018 genus-wide statement.

sources.locator: Section 7 'Prominence', p. 23 (tone inventory in Section 6, pp. 22-23; Azoyú [tpc] listed among sampled varieties in Table 1, p. 4)
sources.note: Sec. 7 'Prominence' p. 23: not clear that anything comparable to stress exists in Me'phaa, but words and phrases are prosodically right-headed; in a disyllabic root the final syllable is strong, the first weak (lenition, historical k>h, b>w, d>r in weak syllables; leftward vowel loss in lexicalized phrases); affixation does not change this. Sec. 6 p. 22-23: three tones (H, M, L) with one- and two-tone melodies; Azoyú [tpc] differs tonally from highland varieties.

sources.citation: Cornelio Tiburcio, Oscar. 2022. El acento y la estructura prosódica en el mè'phàà de la Ciénega del Sauce, Guerrero. Tesis de maestría en Lingüística Indoamericana, CIESAS, Ciudad de México (dir. Hiroto Uchihara). 235 pp.
sources.note: Instrumental + phonological study of an Ayutla (Acatepec-type, not Azoyú) variety: stress is fixed on the last syllable of the phonological word, quantity-insensitive iambic; the only reliable acoustic correlate is lengthening of the onset consonant of the final syllable; vowel length, nasality and contour tones contrast only in the final (tonic) syllable; tones do not affect stress position (pp. 3-4 hypotheses; pp. 171-173 conclusions). Reviews prior claims: Marlett & Weathers 2012/2018 fixed final, Carrasco 2012 ms. fixed final with onset-duration cue, Herrera Zendejas 2018 tone-conditioned.
